Description: An estimated 15,000 to 30,000 clay tablets and fragments forming the administrative archive of the Achaemenid heartland, found in 1933 by Ernst Herzfeld's Oriental Institute expedition in two small rooms of the fortification wall at Persepolis. Most are in Elamite cuneiform, with some Aramaic texts and many uninscribed sealings. They record the intake and distribution of food, livestock, and travel rations across Fars and Elam in the middle of Darius I's reign, about 509-493 BC, under the officials Pharnaces and his deputy Zishshawish.
Interpretations: The tablets are the working paperwork of the empire that let the Jews return from exile and rebuild Jerusalem - the same bureaucracy that issued travel authorisations, rations, and payments to workers. Counts and date ranges vary by source (Livius gives 20,000-25,000 tablets for about 15,000-18,000 documents, dated 506-497 BC); the entry uses the excavators' broader range. They contain no mention of Judah, so they illuminate the Persian world of Ezra and Nehemiah rather than confirming any biblical event.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
BiblicalSignificance: Ezra 6:1 describes a search of the Persian royal archives for Cyrus's decree; the Fortification Tablets are the kind of archive that search would have consulted, showing an empire that ran on written records and stored them for decades.
CurrentLocation: National Museum of Iran, Tehran (majority returned); Oriental Institute, Chicago (remainder)
